endorsements.quote: Evaluating the cognitive transaction under perioperative conditions, not the computational model in isolation, is both a methodological imperative and a patient safety priority.
Adjudicating between formats requires usability testing under simulated time pressure, not static comprehension surveys.
health system informaticists can instrument existing AI tools to capture override rates and response times rather than waiting for purpose-built research infrastructure

unlisted_practices: Study provider-AI disagreement using mixed-methods designs that pair quantitative performance data with structured qualitative inquiry into provider reasoning to distinguish automation bias from legitimate clinical insight.

Study trust calibration longitudinally across repeated clinical encounters, pairing in-the-moment reliance judgments with case-level outcome tracking, rather than using single-session or cross-sectional designs.
Design AI outputs for high-acuity workflows to be low-friction, such as color-coded flags in existing displays or brief prompts delivered at natural pauses, rather than raw probability scores.

Use ecologically valid study designs, such as realistic clinical simulations with eye tracking, to capture provider reasoning under actual perioperative conditions rather than retrospective or survey-based proxies.
Treat human-AI interaction research questions as design requirements to address before deployment rather than as validation exercises conducted afterward.
Engage anesthesia providers in partnership with cognitive psychologists, informaticists, and implementation scientists in developing and evaluating perioperative AI.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/framework paper proposing a human factors research agenda and design considerations for provider-AI cognitive transactions in perioperative and anesthesia care.
